newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian co-PM seeks elections in November 1998.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian co-PM seeks elections in November 1998.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen on Tuesday backed away from recent threats to cancel pending polls and instead proposed holding general elections without foreign help in November 1998.

In a major concession to his political rival and co-premier, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, Hun Sen also said his Cambodian People's Party (CPP) was ready to drop its insistence that members of parliament and government officers must only hold Cambodian passports.

The dual nationality issue had stalled the drafting of an election law, vital for local and general polls due in 1997 and 1998. Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party was strongly opposed to barring returnees with foreign passports from holding power.
"In order to let the elections take place, the Cambodian People's Party will not take the nationality issue and try to put it as an obstacle in the election law," Hun Sen said.
"This is the real good will of the Cambodian People's Party, which takes a bone out of someone's throat," he added in a speech from the provinces aired on his party Apsara radio.
Ranariddh and most top members of his party have dual nationality, while a much smaller number of CPP leaders have more than one passport.

The two parties formed an uneasy coalition in 1993 but have been at loggerheads for more than a year over power-sharing, with FUNCINPEC vainly seeking more power to reflect their narrow win over the incumbent CPP at U.N.-run elections in 1993.

Other factors have exacerbated the ill-feeling. Relations plummeted to a new low earlier this month when Hun Sen warned that he would cancel all elections if King Norodom Sihanouk abdicated to enter politics.
The second prime minister said he would demand that all members of the royal family be barred from politics, setting off a fresh war of words with Ranariddh.

But Hun Sen on Tuesday said his party would "ask the royal government and the national assembly to choose November 1998 to have the national election". He added that he hoped a throne crisis would not arise to postpone the polls.

When asked by Reuters whether he supported the proposal for elections, Ranariddh replied: "November, October, we will see. The two committees are meeting now. I support all elections, free, fair, democratic."
Hun Sen also said Cambodia should manage the elections itself, but some foreigners would be invited as simple observers.
The 1993 polls were organised by the United Nations after years of strife had left the country a shell of its former glory.
Ranariddh has said he would like to see a strong international and U.N. presence during the elections.
